passages.t: Raiders at harvest, and a prophet
passages.happening:
Israel does evil again, and the LORD gives them into the hand of Midian for seven years (verse 1). The people hide in mountain shelters, caves and strongholds (verse 2).

Every time Israel plants its crops, the Midianites, the Amalekites and other peoples of the east come up and spoil them, camping as far as Gaza and leaving no food and no animals (verses 3-4). “For the Midianites came with their livestock and their tents like a great swarm of locusts. They and their camels were innumerable, and they entered the land to ravage it” (verse 5).

“Israel was greatly impoverished by Midian, and the Israelites cried out to the LORD” (verse 6).

This time God first sends a prophet. He reminds them that God brought them out of Egypt, rescued them from all their oppressors and gave them the land, and told them not to fear the gods of the Amorites. “But you did not obey Me” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
The Midianites were a people of the desert lands east and south of Canaan, in northwest Arabia and the Sinai. Moses had once lived among them and married a Midianite woman, but later Israel fought them. Here they come with the Amalekites and ‘the people of the east’, a general name for the desert tribes beyond the Jordan.

Their camels gave them a great advantage. On camels, raiders could cross long stretches of desert quickly and carry plunder away. When camels were first used this widely is debated among historians, but this is one of the Bible's earliest pictures of raiding on camels on a large scale.

The raiders came at harvest. They crossed the Jordan, spread through the Valley of Jezreel and reached as far south as Gaza. They did not come to rule. They came to take or destroy the crops and the flocks, year after year, until Israel was starving. That is why the people hid in caves.

When Israel cries out, God does not send a deliverer at once. He sends a prophet with a reminder. The speech is short, like a charge in a court: what God did, what he asked, and how Israel answered. The chapter records no reply. Before God rescues them, he wants them to know why they needed rescuing.
passages.later:
Israel's later prophets remembered the day God broke Midian's hold as a picture of rescue: “For as in the day of Midian You have shattered the yoke of their burden, the bar across their shoulders, and the rod of their oppressor” (Isaiah 9:4).

The prophet's words echo the opening of the Ten Commandments, which begin with what God had done: ‘I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt’ (Exodus 20:2).
passages.asks: God answered Israel's cry first with a reminder of their disobedience. Ask whether you want God's help more than you want to hear what he has to say about how you got here. And ask what you are hiding in caves from, and whether the trouble you fear is the real enemy.

passages.happening:
The angel of the LORD comes and sits under an oak at Ophrah, where Gideon son of Joash is threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites (verse 11). “The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor” (verse 12).

Gideon answers honestly, and a little bitterly. “Please, my Lord,” Gideon replied, “if the LORD is with us, why has all this happened to us? And where are all His wonders of which our fathers told us” (verse 13). He says that the LORD has abandoned them.

“Go in the strength you have and save Israel from the hand of Midian. Am I not sending you?” (verse 14). Gideon objects that his clan is the weakest in Manasseh and he is the youngest in his father's house. “Surely I will be with you,” the LORD replied (verse 16).

Gideon asks for a sign and brings an offering of meat and bread. The angel touches it with the tip of his staff, fire flares from the rock and burns it up, and the angel vanishes (verses 17-21). Gideon is terrified. He has seen the angel of the LORD face to face. “Peace be with you. Do not be afraid, for you will not die” (verse 23). Gideon builds an altar there and calls it The LORD Is Peace (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Wheat was normally threshed on an open, raised floor of rock or beaten earth, where the wind could carry the chaff away when the grain was tossed in the air. A winepress was a pit cut in the rock for treading grapes, low and hidden. It was the worst place to thresh and the best place to hide. The first thing the story tells about Gideon is how afraid his whole country was.

So the angel's greeting, ‘O mighty man of valor’, sounds almost like a joke. But it names what God means to make of him.

The scene follows the pattern of the call of Moses at the burning bush: God meets a man, sends him, hears his objection that he is too weak, promises ‘I will be with you’, and gives a sign. Gideon's questions are honest. If the LORD is with his people, where are the wonders their fathers told them about? The Bible does not rebuke him for asking.

Gideon calls himself the least of the least. God does not argue with that. He answers with his own presence: ‘I will be with you’.

People believed that to see God, or even his angel, face to face would bring death. That is why Gideon panics. God's answer is peace. The name of the altar joins the name of the LORD with shalom, the Hebrew word for peace, wholeness and well-being. A man who expected to die names the place for the peace he was given.
passages.later:
The call of Moses has the same shape. Moses asked, “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?” and God answered, “I will surely be with you” (Exodus 3:11-12).

The fear of seeing God goes back to Sinai: “You cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live” (Exodus 33:20).

Gideon is named in the letter to the Hebrews among those who acted by faith (Hebrews 11:32), faith that was often weak, as this chapter shows, but real.
passages.hard:
Who appeared to Gideon, an angel or the LORD himself?

The text moves between the two. It says ‘the angel of the LORD’ appeared (verse 12), and then ‘The LORD turned to him and said’ (verse 14). Gideon fears death because he has seen the angel of the LORD face to face.

Readers have understood this in more than one way, as with the angel at Bochim in chapter 2. Many Christian interpreters have seen an appearance of God the Son before he was born as a man. Others read a created messenger who bears God's name and speaks with his full authority, so that meeting him is like meeting God. These notes do not choose between these readings. The chapter's point is clear on any of them: God himself came to call a frightened man, and his presence brought peace.
passages.asks: God called a frightened man hiding his grain, and he did not wait for Gideon to stop being afraid. Ask what God might be calling you to do ‘in the strength you have’, not the strength you wish you had. And hear Gideon's honest question. Ask whether you bring God your real questions, or only the polite ones.

passages.t: Baal's altar torn down at night
passages.happening:
That night the LORD tells Gideon to take his father's bull, tear down his father's altar to Baal, cut down the Asherah pole beside it, and build a proper altar to the LORD (verses 25-26).

Gideon does it with ten of his servants. But because he is afraid of his family and the men of the town, he does it by night (verse 27).

In the morning the townsmen find the altar torn down and ask who did it. They are told it was Gideon, and they demand his death (verses 28-30).

His father Joash answers them. “Are you contending for Baal? Are you trying to save him?” (verse 31). If Baal is a god, let him fight for himself. So Gideon is called Jerubbaal, “Let Baal contend with him” (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
Before Gideon can fight Midian, he has to face Baal in his own father's house. The altar to Baal belonged to Gideon's family, and the town treated it as its own. That shows how deeply the worship of Canaan had taken root inside Israel. The trouble outside and the unfaithfulness inside were bound together.

An Asherah pole was a wooden object set up for the goddess Asherah, often beside an altar.

Gideon obeys, but fearfully. He goes at night. The Bible does not hide that, and it does not scold him for it either. Obedience done afraid is still obedience.

The men of the town want to kill him for insulting Baal. It is a measure of how far things had gone that Israelites would put a man to death for tearing down an altar the law of Moses had told them to destroy.

Joash's answer is shrewd. A real god would not need men to defend him. The Hebrew verb he uses means to plead a case or contend, and it becomes Gideon's new name, Jerubbaal, ‘Let Baal contend with him’. The name is a standing challenge to a god who could not defend his own altar.
passages.later:
Samuel later remembered Gideon by this name: “So the LORD sent Jerubbaal, Barak, Jephthah, and Samuel, and He delivered you from the hands of your enemies on every side” (1 Samuel 12:11).

The same question, whether a god can answer for himself, is put to the test on Mount Carmel, when Elijah mocks the prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18:27).
passages.asks: Gideon's first battle was in his own family's backyard. Ask what idols are closest to home for you, the things your family or your town treats as untouchable. And notice that Gideon obeyed at night, afraid. Ask whether there is something God has told you to do that you could do today, even afraid.

passages.happening:
The Midianites, the Amalekites and the peoples of the east gather, cross the Jordan and camp in the Valley of Jezreel (verse 33). “So the Spirit of the LORD came upon Gideon, who blew the ram’s horn and rallied the Abiezrites behind him” (verse 34). He sends messengers through Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun and Naphtali, and they come (verse 35).

Then Gideon asks God for a sign. He will put a fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If dew falls only on the fleece and the ground stays dry, he will know God will save Israel by his hand. So it happens, and he wrings a bowlful of water from the fleece (verses 36-38).

“Do not be angry with me; let me speak one more time” (verse 39). This time, he asks, let the fleece be dry and the ground wet. That night God does so (verse 40).
passages.hearers:
The Spirit of the LORD came upon Gideon. The Hebrew says, vividly, that the Spirit clothed himself with Gideon. A timid man is given strength to lead, and the tribes answer his call.

Then comes the fleece, and the order matters. God had already promised victory (verse 16), had given a sign at the rock (verse 21), and now his Spirit had come on Gideon (verse 34). Still Gideon asks for more. The writer places the fleece after the Spirit, and a reader is meant to wonder why he still needs a sign.

The test made use of the heavy dew that falls in the land during the dry season, enough to soak wool overnight. The first sign could be explained: wool holds dew. So Gideon asks for the harder one, a dry fleece on wet ground. He knows he is pressing his request, and he asks God not to be angry.

God answers both times. The story shows a God who stoops to strengthen weak faith.
passages.later: The law had said, “Do not test the LORD your God as you tested Him at Massah” (Deuteronomy 6:16), and Jesus answered the tempter with the same words: “It is also written: ‘Do not put the Lord your God to the test’” (Matthew 4:7).
passages.hard:
Was Gideon wrong to test God with the fleece, and should Christians put out a fleece today?

Gideon asked after God had already promised victory and after the Spirit had come on him. So many readers see the fleece as a sign of weak faith rather than a model to follow. The law warns against putting God to the test, and Gideon himself seems to know it, since he asks God not to be angry.

Other readers stress that God answered him graciously, and see the story as a picture of God's patience with people who are afraid.

Most agree that the passage tells what Gideon did and does not prescribe a way of seeking God's guidance. Christians differ on whether it is right to ask God for signs when making decisions. But the heart of the story is not the fleece. It is a God who bears with a fearful man's need for reassurance.
passages.asks: Gideon had God's word and God's Spirit, and he still wanted the dew to prove it. Ask what you are asking God to prove that he has already said. Then take comfort where the story does. Ask how it changes your fear to know that God answered Gideon twice, and was not angry.
